That forced me to use a database, because now I could use triggers to automatically save off old values, and views to use them nicely.

There were many Python SQLite wrappers at the time, but I didn't like them. So I wrote another one :)

https://www.rogerbinns.com/blog/20-years-of-apsw.html

(I am the APSW maintainer)

Same experience here, from a multiplayer game server. Go, one SQLite file per game world, one process owns each file, all on a local SSD.

In a load test with 512 players all active on one world, command acks were 4-6 ms at the median and under 50 ms at p95, on a single Ryzen 9 3900X box. And most of that time is game logic and fanning out updates over websockets, not the database.

The part people worry about is durability, because SSDs have limited write cycles. So I took care to have backups of the state, recovery in short time etc.

I stream the WAL to object storage with Litestream, with one gotcha: I had to turn off SQLite’s own auto-checkpoint and let only Litestream checkpoint, or the two step on each other.

You said a lot and I don't want this to turn into a wall of zig-zagging tit for tat nonsense, so I just want to speak briefly and holistically. The first missions to Mars will be fully dependent upon supplies we're bringing. The goal of self sustainability is aspirational and long-term. At best it will take decades. In reality, it may never happen much in the same way that no country in the world today is fully self sustainable in practice, even if many could be in theory.

The whole point of the extended stays in LEO are precisely to simulate worse case scenarios for travel to Mars. So for instance the record for the longest time in space is held by Valeri Polyakov. [1] He spent 437 days on Mir in LEO, and then opted to immediately walk upon landing back on Earth. It was all to prove that humans would be physically capable of working on Mars (which has 1/3rd the gravity of Earth) even after absurdly long periods of time in space. In fact his first words upon return from his first (240 day) stay in space were "We can fly to Mars."

Robotics don't really work well for space exploration, because moving parts break. For instance the Curiosity/Perseverance drills are cutting edge yet have a max depth of ~2.7 inches. And traveling is even harder. On average Curiosity ended up traveling about 1 mile per year. It's all because if anything breaks, that's game over. So everything has to be done with the utmost of caution, and even then stuff constantly breaks. Curiosity's drill broke after about a dozen activations and required a team of scientists and months of full-time work to create a passable work-around when it could have viably been fixed on the ground by a human in a few moments.

This is part of the reason that we only learned in 2013 that the soil/regolith on Mars is actually extremely moist, 2-5% water by volume. A cubic foot of soil heated up gets you about 2 pints, a liter, of water. The whole plot-line in "The Martian" about having to jump through hoops to get water was correct based on the latest knowledge when the book was written in 2011. We'll probably learn more in a couple of weeks with people on Mars than we have with 60 years of probes and rovers.

I'm certain every human of sound mind is grateful for Earth. That's not a reason to not seek to expand out as far and as wide as we can.

Rust is specifically designed to ensure that safe code can never trigger UB (barring compiler bugs, or bugs in unsafe code blocks). For that, protecting against races is necessary (at least when using LLVM as a backend, and when using the C++ memory model).

In practice rust also tries to guide you towards patterns that reduces the risk of other bugs. For example, using Result, Option (and enums in general) reduces the risk that you forget to handle error paths. It is also quite hard to get memory leaks unintentionally in Rust, since by default you work with various smart pointers.

In my experience typical multi-threaded C++ has a lot of threading bugs that tend to cause hard to reproduce bugs (I work in safety critical hard realtime robotics / machine control, where we have a lot of communicating threads). When I code Rust I can trust the language to prevent those classes of bugs, letting me focus on the actual hard domain specific problems, rather than language minutiae. Yes, TSAN helps in C++, but that is dynamic analysis so it has to actually catch the potential problem happening while running.

So I think that the multithreading approach in Rust is really good and what we want, not a hindrance. It is absolutely the right thing to do.

Now, the async story is another matter and I have conflicting opinions on how that is done in rust. I can't think of a significantly better design that would work on microcontrollers / no-std though. I'm not interested in anything that requires allocations or a runtime.
